decisions.quote: In replicating and extending Haun et al. (Experiment 1), English- but not Tseltal-speaking children could use their language-incongruent system when the instructions used their non-preferred frame of reference. Perseveration due to task order may explain the discrepancies between present English- and previous Dutch-speaking children, while not understanding task instructions using left/right language may explain why present Tseltal- and previous Hai||om-speaking children had difficulty with their language-incongruent systems.
decisions.reason: In the supplied abstract-only source, Haun et al. (2011) found that both Dutch-speaking (egocentric) and Hai||om-speaking (geocentric) children had difficulty using their language-incongruent reference frame. In Experiment 1 (the replication), this difficulty held for Tseltal-speaking children (matching Hai||om-speaking children) but not for English-speaking children, which the authors explicitly describe as 'discrepancies between present English- and previous Dutch-speaking children.' Under the codebook, 'statistically successful but flawed' requires both that the original empirical effect was obtained and that the main message argues the method does not validly test the hypothesis. Neither requirement holds in the abstract: first, the original cross-group effect was only partially recovered in Experiment 1 rather than obtained in full (the shipped 'successful' quote comes from full text absent from the source); second, task order and instruction comprehension are proposed cautiously ('may explain') and tested via follow-up extension experiments (Experiments 2-5) to reconcile conflicting literature under a competing causal account ('suggest that task constraints, rather than language, determine which system is easier to use'). Because Experiment 1 reports one agreeing comparison and one explicit discrepancy with the original study, the outcome is 'mixed'.

scope_review.parent_objection: First reply codes mixed across English versus original Dutch discrepancy and Tseltal versus Hai||om agreement. But abstract main conclusion says task constraints rather than language determine reference-frame performance; later experiments reproduce Tseltal ability when task instructions no longer use unfamiliar left/right language. Does this constitute main methodological-validity critique of original language-relative-hypothesis test, supporting statistically successful but flawed, or ordinary partial replication mixed with explanatory/extension experiments? Apply exact special-category rule: original effect obtained AND main argument method does not validly test hypothesis; cautious possible explanations alone not enough. Source is abstract-only. Explain whether original empirical effect recovered enough and critique is actually asserted as invalid-test main message, not just competing causal interpretation. Otherwise retain mixed or undeterminable with source scope.

prior_reply.reason: Whereas Haun et al. (2011) found that both Dutch- and Hai||om-speaking children had difficulty using their language-incongruent spatial reference frame, Experiment 1 replicated this difficulty for Tseltal-speaking children but found a discrepancy for English-speaking children, who could use their language-incongruent system. Because one comparison agrees with the original finding and the other explicitly diverges, the replication outcome is mixed.
